A full township provides 64 free homesteads. The townships to be subdivided during the present season are situated between Fort Pelly in eastern Assiniboia and Edmonton in Alberta. Some are on bare prairie and some in country more or less wooded. The intention is to survey about 500 townships. Four hundred are estimated to cost about $900 each. The remaining one hundred townships, being more heavily wooded, are estimated at $1,200 each.
If I understand it correctly, all the mapping out work is done by men paid by the day ?

The general principle is that the outline work is done by surveyors under pay, and township subdividing is done by surveyors who are under contract where the nature of the work is such that the cost can be fully estimated.
What is paid per day for outlining work laying out the townships ?

We are doing that work under charge of Dominion land surveyors, who receive $6.50 per day, assistants, who receive $3 per day, and labourers, who are paid the rate of' wages of the locality. The ordinary party consists of a land surveyor, his assistant,, nine or ten labourers and a cook. I may say that the rate of pay for surveyors is greater of late years. Had we not increased the rate of pay we were likely to be left without good surveyors, and some time ago the pay was increased from $5 to $6.50 on the advice of the Surveyor General. We have practically all, or nearly, all the available Dominion land surveyors working for the department.
In addition to their pay, these parties are found, they are supplied?:
Yes.

The hon. minister proposes to survey 500 townships, most of the work to be done under contract. But, practically, there is no competition in that work, because the hon. minister fixes the pay that is allowed for prairie sections, wooded sections, and so on. So, it is difficult to ascertain what the ordinary cost of subdividing these townships is.

This has all been Worked out carefully by the Surveyor General. He has not only his own experience to go by, but he has the results of survey work in that country for the last twenty-five years, showing just what it costs in different cases, so that he can work out schedules for the several sections.
Are the surveyors who work under contract found also ?
When a surveyor takes a contract, he furnishes his own supplies. But, when he is under daily pay, the government finds him.
Is the land surveyed pretty well taken up ? For it would appear that the government is mapping out a very large summer's work-500 townships.

My hon. friend will see that we have not mapped out more than is necessary. Five hundred townships would give only 32,000 homesteads, and we had 31,000 homesteads taken up last year. Practically the surveys are getting pretty closely run. It is difficult to keep ahead of settlement. But it is important to keep ahead, for most unsatisfactory results follow if settlers go in in advance of the surveys. The people get on odd numbered sections, or school sections, two men take up the same quarter-section, and in many other ways most unsatisfactory conditions arise.

It is partly curiosity that induced me to make these inquiries. I have some remembrance of a strong criticism made against the old government for surveying too much and spending too heavily. The hon. minister is asking now about three-quarters of a million for surveys this year. That, I think, is very much more than ever was asked for this service before. In connection with that is the fact which is disclosed by the minister just now, that we have a lot of surveyed townships already, because a portion of that is to be taken for retracing these lines. He did not tell us how much of this expenditure would be incurred in that work. We find that $10,000 of this is for the purpose of inspecting surveys. Is that inspection to be done at Ottawa or to be done in the country, and what is the necessity for that inspection ?

A portion of this money is to be employed in renewing the obliterated marks of previous surveys. There are two parties now at work, and it is estimated that they will be able to renew surveyed lines in about thirty townships, at an average cost of about $5 per mile. I -may say that so far back as the time of the government of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie, mistakes were made in pushing surveys where they were not necessary, and surveyors were sent out during a number of years to survey lands which did not need to be surveyed. We have never got any value from some of those surveys. I do not mean to say that the largest portion of the work is to be characterized in that way. but I say that a mistake was made in the beginning. I do not think that any of the ministers in particular were to blame, because they were acting under the advice of their officers who were supposed to be familiar with the country. But there is no doubt that they did survey quantities of land which were not fit for settlement. We find ourselves that it is a difficult matter and requires careful examination and supervision to select the land that ought to be surveyed. We have an inspector of surveys and an assistant inspector, who make a careful inspection of the land that they think ought to be surveyed. Mr. Pearce, now the inspector of surveys, is a very old officer of the government, and I regret to say that he has applied to be placed upon the retired list. He is a very competent man. He and hisi assistant came down here early in the session and went carefully into the whole subject with me, and made recommendations to the department as to the land that should be surveyed. I am satisfied that we are not surveying a particle more this year than is absolutely needed for settlement.

Is it the policy of the government to select in each locality only such land as will be required for settlement, and to leave patches of unsurveyed land ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, Our policy is to select lands that we think the settlers are likely to desire to settle upon. Settlement is moving forward in^ certain districts, and when our officers report to us that settlers are going to certain districts, we take measures to survey the land so that it may be ready for them when they wish to make their entries.
I did not understand how the minister determines that amount of pay that is to be given.
We act absolutely upon the advice of the surveyor general. We do not pretend to know anything about it, and rely entirely upon the officers of the Survey Department.
Who fixes the price to be paid per mile for every survey that is made ?
The Governor General decides it on my recommendation, and I make my recommendation on the advice of the surveyor general.

How much is allowed for supplies to those who are engaged by the department ?
The MINISTER! OF THE INTERIOR. I am informed that fifty cents a day is allowed to each man for maintenance. That is all they get, except the salary.

My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Roche) made a couple of motions for returns which I understand have not yet been brought down. Perhaps the attention of the minister has been drawn to them. They ought to have been before

the House before this. They had reference to the odd sections of lands that X believe are reserved for settlers going into the country, the other sections being granted to the Manitoba and Saskatchewan Railway Company. His motion asked for the price 'being paid per acre. I cannot understand that any such sale should have been made, because I do not see any authority under the law,to allow the minister to do it.
Does my hon. friend say there was a motion for a return ?
Yes. It must have been on the Order paper for eight or ten weeks.
Then my attention has not been called to it. Is the hon. gentleman sure it was not a question ?
There was both a motion and a question.
If it is a return, I will have it brought down to-morrow, because it can be prepared in a Short time.

I would just like to say in connection with the amount of money being paid for this work to-day, while I am not objecting to it, because it is pretty costly to live in that country, I have a very distinct recollection of strong complaints being made because the late government paid $5 a day for their surveyors while the present government, whose friends so strongly objected to it, sit in the House today and are quite willing to defend paying $6.50 a day, showing that the rigid economy for which they were so noted in the past evaporated, when they got on the treasury benches.
It is a growing time.

And that was in a new era of the country when transportation was difficult and expensive and the cost of living was high. Surely, with the settlement of the country through the lapse of years since then, provisions ought to be a little cheaper, transportation ought to be a little cheaper and a little more convenient, and if these considerations were an ample justification for the expense then, that reason does not exist to-day. But, notwithstanding that fact the government are paying very much more for this service. The hon. minister says that this is a growing time. Well, it seems to be a growing time in most lines except in cabinet ministers. In that regard there appears to be a shrinkage lately and I am inclined to think there will be other experiences of the kind described by Artemus Ward when he said that when one commences to go down hill it would seem as if all nature had been Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
greased for the occasion to let you slide. I think they will find it so in their exjieri-ence as well.
I see that there is a vote of $13,000 for surveyors for irri gation purposes. I would like to know what has been done in the past in regard to surveys for irrigation purposes.

Irrigation surveys have been carried on for a considerable number of years. If my recollection serves me right they were begun some time about 1891 or 1892; at any rate, some years before I took office. They were carried on for a number of years under the supervision of Mr. J. S. Dennis, who, under the late government, was the inspector of surveys, and who held the position which is now held by Mr. Wm. Pearce. Mr. Dennis shortly after I took office, resigned and became the deputy commissioner of Public Works under the North-west Territorial government. The surveys had been carried on for a number of years by Mr. Dennis and as he was a most competent person, in fact, practically the only man in the service who had a knowledge of the subject, I made aD arrangement under which, while he remained the deputy commissioner of Public Works in the North-west Territories, and was not really in the service of the federal government, he should supervise the irrigation work and the work of the staff. That plan has been carried on and it has been found a very desirable plan to follow by reason of the fact that irrigation in the North-west Territories is controlled by legislation which is administered to a considerable extent by the local officers, and ft is desirable that we should act with the officers of the Territorial government in administering our irrigation survey work. We have voted $13,000 per year for irrigation surveys and a very valuable amount of information has been collected. A very extensive system of records has been prepared, although, of course, that does not by any means exhaust the possibilities of procuring information in that vast country; yet a substantial beginning has been made. Thanks very largely to the interest, enthusiasm and ability of Mr. Dennis we have succeeded in laying the foundation of a very thorough system of irrigation surveys.
Have there been any irrigation works carried out ?

Yes, irrigation works have been carried out and if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Smith, Wentworth) will consult legislation upon this subject he will find an Act of this parliament which provides the method under which water rights can be procured. We have provided a method by which we can sell lands to applicants who desire to irrigate the land. Parties make application to the local authorities to get irrigating rights

and then they proceed to do the work. I could not at* this moment give my hon. friend the statistics in regard to the amount of irrigation that has been done. That can be easily procured if my hon. friend is desirous of having it. We have not given any government assistance directly in the way of bonus for the purpose of doing irrigation work. We have contented ourselves with acquiring information and written records in regard to that work by procuring surveys to be made, so that when parties desire to do irrigation work they can get the necessary information in regard to levels and the flow of water and that sort of thing by consulting the irrigation officers. One irrigation project has been to some extent carried into effect near Calgary. Another very large system of irrigation has been carried into effect by what is known as the Alberta Irrigation Company, the president of which is Mr. E. T. Galt, of Montreal. They have 100 miles of a water course. I have had the pleasure of seeing this work and it has practically transformed the whole district through which it runs. Large settlements have been brought in and people are going in there now. It is in the neighbourhood of Lethbridge. If my hon. friend has paid any attention to the reports from that part of the country he will have seen that as a result of this irrigation scheme, which is about to be extended, a large settlement has been brought into the neighbourhood of Lethbridge and a beetroot sugar factory has been started on a large scale, with the result that we shall not only have farming but manufacturing industries carried on to a very considerable extent. I think the result is directly due to the inauguration of irrigation work by the government some years ago.
Dominion lands-chargeable to income-commissioner's salary, $3,000.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
I will give a general explanation of the charges in the vote for Dominion lands.

Who is the superintendent of mines ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Dr. Haanel.

He is in the department here '!
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Yes. As to the increase of $12,000 in the salaries of inspectors and so on, I may say that since these estimates were made up there has been such an unprecedented tide of immigration that it was impossible to keep the work up with the existing staff,-and so others had to be employed. There is a vote of $8,000 in the supplementary estimates and the same explanation will apply to that.
Inspector's expenses, travelling expenses of commissioner, superintendent of mines and
homestead inspectors, contingencies of Dominion lands and crown timber agents and at head office, removal expenses, stationery and printing, &=., $37,100.
How do you determine what amount is to be paid in travelling expenses.

In all cases at present we pay actual expenses. They have to return vouchers for every dollar expended. Formerly they were allowed so much per day for expenses and I think the homestead inspectors were allowed so much per year. But now we require vouchers no matter how small the amount, except it is in the nature of a payment for which a voucher cannot be produced and then the inspector requires evidence, that the money was paid and he audits the accounts and they are afterwards submitted to the Auditor General.
What is meant by removal expenses ?
If an officer should be removed from one district to another and if under the Order in Council we are liable to pay his moving expenses it is paid out of this money.

IIow is that Order in Council regulated ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
If he gets an increase of salary on account of removal he does not get his expenses but otherwise he does.

Would this item cover the case of a person who is appointed to a position in the Yukon from Ontario.
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
No.

What is the practice of the department in that regard ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR,
My deputy informs me that the expenses are not paid except in the case of an officer who was in the service here or in some other part of the country who is sent out to a distant place. In the case of a man being newly appointed to the service his expenses are not paid.
I do not think there is much objection to that.
Would the minister be good enough to explain what the removal expenses are ?

There is an increase in this vote altogether of $4,000. The items that are paid out of it are the homestead inspectors' expenses, forest rangers' expenses, the travelling expenses of officers of that branch of the department, like the Commissioner of Dominion Lands, removal and attendance expenses of officers of the outside service,

printing and stationery for the Crown lands and timber agencies, expenses for temporary assistance at the agencies when any is required, and a small amount paid for commissions on permits, where commissions are allowed by the department.
What are the duties of the homestead inspectors ?

The homestead inspectors have to report generally upon every item of information that is required by the department. But their primary and most important duty is to see to the performance of the homestead duties required by the Dominion Lands Act from homesteaders. No homesteader can get a patent for his land until the homestead inspector has made a report to the department after a personal visit to the homestead. He is notified from time to time by the land office of the applications for patents as they come in, and then he visits the homesteads of the different applicants, takes the necessary affidavits, and makes his report with the evidence to the department. This is laid before the Commissioner of Dominion lands, and the application is approved or otherwise.
About how many homestead inspectors are there ?

Nineteen at present. I may say that the Commissioner of Dominion lands reports to me that it will be absolutely impossible for him to keep up the work with this number, and he has recommended that we should have at least three or four more.
I suppose their duties take their whole time ?
They work under the Inspector of Dominion lands, at Winnipeg, and under the rules and regulations they have to account to him for every day of the year.

Will the hon. minister explain what duties are performed at the Dominion lands office at Winnipeg, and what lands are disposed of there ? If one wants to buy land, has he to go to the Winnipeg office ?
The Winnipeg office is not different from any other land office.
Is it not more expensive to keep up than the Edmonton or the Calgary office ?

I fancy it is. That is owing to the interminable complications that have arisen in connection with the patents for river lots along the Red river. There is a vast amount of work done at the Winnipeg office in connection with these that is not done at other offices. Officials have been Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
kept there under considerable salary for no other reason than that they knew the location of the river lots, and knew how they were drawn. The administration of the law with regard to these river lots is very tangled and very difficult, and is proportionately expensive.
I notice a large sum down for surveys. Is the minister doing anything in the country beyond Edmonton, towards the Peace river ?

Not very much. We have one party there, but that is all. The policy of the department is not to do very much in that direction. My hon. friend is familiar enough with the west to know that some people have the notion to go as far away as they can. It is the policy of the department to get the nearest land settled up first, and I do not think it would be wise for us to survey the Peace river country when there is so much land nearer that is yet unsettled.

I find in the Auditor General's Report L-25 and continuing on. probably a dozen pages, many entries of payments to different parties for services in inspection of lands or as land guides. These run into thousands of dollars. Does not every surveyor, after the completion of his work, deposit in the department an accurate description of each section of land ? If that be the case, every land agent at these different points should be furnished with a schedule describing these different sections. If access can be had to these, why is it necessary to send out guides witn the settlers ? Not only are fees paid to those so-called land guides, but hundreds of dollars are paid for livery hire. That must give the hon. minister an immense amount of patronage to distribute among his friends.

It is true that the surveyor furnishes an accurate record to the department of his, surveys and it is also true that the local agents of the Dominion are given that information. Not only is that the case, but we have small printed mails giving copies of field notes. But I may say to my hon. friend, that does not at all take away the necessity of giving constant assistance to incoming settlers in the way of locating them. A stranger not accustomed to travelling on the prairies and to our methods of survey, is very hopeless when he gets to locate, and we have found one of the most pressing needs of immigration work to be the furnishing of efficient guides to locate the settlers. It is quite true that the hiring of livery rigs places in my hands a considerable amount of patronage, but if my hon. friend had to administer it. he would find that with three or four livery stables in a small town all wanting patronage, he would have considerable difficulty

oil his hands, and I should be quite willing to transfer that particular patronage to my bon. friend. But these guides are absolutely necessary because the average settler, unfamiliar with our system of survey, find it totally impossible to discover his section.
What is the usual practice ? Do the settlers first go out with the guides aud look over the lands and then come to the office of the agent to see where that land is ?

That is managed through the immigration commissioner at Winnipeg. In certain districts the land agents are given the services of guides. When a settler comes to the land oflice and asks for a guide, a guide is sent out with him. Sometimes a guide is sent out with a party of people. The commissioner is governed by the circumstances. There is no fixed rule, but the object is to assist new settlers to pick out the land they want with the least possible expenditure of time and money.

The coloured township maps now issued do not show the quality of the land, and one has to go to the field to find that out. It would be just as easy to have the quality of the land described on these maps as not.
I thought that was done. It used to be done.

It is not done. The general characteristics of the country are marked but not the quality of the land. When a man pays fifty cents for a map, he wants to get all the information possible out of it. Many persons in Ontario and elsewhere, who wish to select an area in which to settle, do not know the parts already homesteaded and the parts where they may take out homestead entries. It would be easy for the department to issue parti-coloured maps, showing the sections still open for homesteads. All the railways now issue section maps.

That would be very difficult. The result would be this :	A man would get his map
and see a certain piece of land marked upon it open for homestead. He would travel four or five hundred miles for the purpose of location, and then find somebody else there. He would then have a bill of damages against the department. The bill might be unreasonable, but the man would ask the department to pay it. Such claims would be coming in constantly.
Does lie ask the Canadian Pacific Railway to pay it ?
The Canadian Pacific Railway is not the government.

How much approximately was paid out for these so-called land guides ? One man, James Thompson, drew no less a sum than $714 ; another $274, and another $126. These items are found all through the report. When a man buys from the Canadian Pacific Railway, he simply takes advantage of the field uotes furnished him. Do the settlers go out in the first instance with the guide to see the land or do they first locate on the strength of the report in the department office and then go out with the guide ?

There are no absolutely hard and fast rules. When a settler comes to the laud office for information, the land agent shows him the reports and tells him to go out aud locate his land, but he does not know how to get there, and when he does get there, he does not know whether he is on a railway section or where he is. I can assure my hon. friend that there is no part of the service in connection with immigration and land office work that. is more absolutely essential than the sending out of guides to assist new settlers to locate. If it were not done, we should find the settlers congregated about the railway station or the land office, not knowing where to go or what to do.

It seems very odd, if we have an intelligent people going into that country, that such assistance should be necessary. When they go into the office and are handed a map-as they must be if they inquire for one-and the direction is indicated in which they are to look for their land, I should think it would be easy, with the simple system of surveys that is carried on in the North-west (all the lands being in squares) to locate their land. I have never done work of that kind, but I have been told repeatedly by men who have bought lands from the Canadian Pacific Railway that they go to the office and get the field notes, showing where these lands are that are available. They go out of their own accord and find no difficulty in locating the land still unsold. Then they come back, compare their notes with the notes in the office and decide whether or not they wish to purchase. Can the hon. minister tell me how many thousands of dollars have been spent last year approximately, on these so-called land guides 7

I am not able to give the hon. gentleman a correct statement now, and an incorrect statement would be worse than none. But I will be able to give him the facts in a couple of days. I will have a statement prepared. With regard to the information he has received, I have known my. hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) a considerable while and consider him a man of reasonable capacity in these matters. But I venture to say that if he had to go and pick out land, hav-

ing no guide and only the information given him in a land office to go by, he would be a long time finding his land. I may say I tried it myself. I do not profess to have a very extraordinary degree of knowledge on these matters, but I have lived long enough in that country to know something of the difficulties. The ordinary man not familiar with land hunting and land examining is almost helpless when he goes out on the prairies, so far as finding any particular piece of land is concerned. My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) is familiar with that country and I have never spoken to him on this subject, but I venture to say that if he is asked he will corroborate what I say. There is nothing I am surer about than the absolute necessity of this class of service.
Has the government the land for sale, or only land for homesteading ?

It is against the policy of the department to sell, generally speaking. Until three or four years ago sales were made from time to time, but not of an important character. But even small sales are discontinued and are discouraged by the department. Exceptions are made in special cases. For instance, a man may have lost his homestead through being financially unfortunate. If he could not acquire another farm upon terms within his reach, he would go out of the country and would be lost to us. In such a case, if an application is made and the facts are proven before our officer, we may sell a quarter, section at a low figure-$2 or $3 an acre. Land not of good quality is sold at as low as $1 an acre. These sales are always in the case of actual settlers, to give a man the same chance as would be given him by allowing him to take up another homestead. The law does not permit a second homestead, so we attain some degree of flexibility in the management of the land by having the sales made in this way. Or, sometimes, men who have engaged in ranching make application to buy small quantities of land; I may say they generally want as much as they can get. Sometimes, owing to changes going on in the country the rancher's property would be destroyed if he were not able to protect himself by purchasing the land. A man may have started a cattle industry and put up buildings and find that he is running his cattle on the public domain. Unless he can get some basis for the industry he would be wiped out. In a few cases of that kind, after looking into the matter carefully, we sell small quantities of land. I think three sections is the most we have sold to one purchaser, and that only after careful investigation. There is a vast quantity of land in the odd numbered sections in the hands of railway companies and land companies, and any one who wants to buy land Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
can buy it-there is any quantity for sale. When we are asked to sell land, our ordinary answer is that we cannot sell, but if the parties wish to buy they can buy it from the companies.
Has the government been making sales of large quantities of land '!

Only in one case, the one to which, no doubt, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox) refers- except in connection with irrigation work. In connection with these works, we have sold considerable quantities. The only other sale of large quantity is that of which I speak, the sale to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company, to which reference was made by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart). While I was away, the officers of the department made an examina-tin of an area some 250,000 acres, in what was regarded as an arid and practically useless section. The land was sold at .$1 per acre, upon settlement conditions. I will bring down full particulars before my estimates are fully disposed of.
Does the minister, or does the government, take any cognizance of the construction of roads in the North-west ?

We have not any vote for the construction of roads in the estimates this year. I do not remember that we have ever had any such votes except on one or two occasions. When money was voted for roads in the northern portion of the country. If I remember well, we once voted money for the construction of a road in the Peace River district in the neighbourhood of Dunvegan, which was constructed under the supervision of the Commissioner of Public Works for the North-west Territories. Then four or five thousand dollars were voted for a road near Green lake, west of Prince Albert.

I would impress upon the minister the necessity of constructing roads, or assisting in constructing them by increasing the grant to the territorial government. As my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver) knows, there are many places where the settlers have long distances to haul their grain, and the roads are very bad. It would answer the purpose as well if the money were handed over to the territorial government and they were encouraged to build the roads.
I will go into that somewhat fully when we come to the vote for the North-west Territories.

I do not know whether it is exactly germane to this vote, but I notice that in the list of amounts paid over to various denominations in connection with the half-breed schools in the North-

west as given in the Auditor General's Report, some teachers receive very low salaries, and others very high salaries, comparatively speaking.
Is the hon. gentleman able to tell us how much land is still available for settlement by means of homestead. entries in the four organized territories ?
I will give that information on some other item later on.

The hon. gentleman will find the items I mentioned on pages L-40 and L-41. The amounts are not nearly the same. The point I make is, Why is there a discrepancy in the sums paid to the various teachers ? Why are they not all paid the same amounts ? The hon. gentleman will notice that the Protestant schools get comparatively small sums, or nothing whatever, $100, $50, $75. $200 ; whereas the Roman Catholic schools get $400 and $500.

This vote has always been administered by the Lieutenant Governor of the North-west Territories. There has been no change. We grant a certain sum of money, and the Lieutenant Governor distributes it in assisting schools in the unorganized districts. This department has never had any supervision over it.
But the minister has received a report of the administration of the money ?

Yes, I have a report; but it only shows what is paid in the unorganized districts each year, the grant payable to each school, and when last paid. Nine of the schools are Episcopalian, 12 are Roman Catholic. No other denomination is represented. I would gather from the statements that the difference in salary is due to the fact that some teachers are employed a longer time than others.

I think the minister should look into this matter a little more closely.

Protection ol timber lands in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and tree culture in the North-west Territories, $25,000.
' Mr. TAYLOR. The vote last year was $15,000. Would the hon. minister kindly explain the reason for this increase of $10.000 over last year's estimate ? I would like the hon. minister to explain what benefits we are receiving from tree culture.

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) that the increase is caused by an increase in the scope of the work. We started in a comparatively small way and we are operating in a comparatively small way yet, and I am only sorry that we have not been able to ask for a larger amount of money to be devoted to this purpose. I may say to my hon. friends that if they read the report of the superintendent of forestry explaining that work they will understand what has been done. I am told that he appeared before the Committee on Agriculture and explained very fully the scope of his operations and therefore it is unnecessary for me to repeat the statement here.
I suppose the hon. minister refers to Mr. Stewart ?
Yes.
I did not happen to be at the committee, and I would like to hear what Mr. Stewart's salary is and what his duties are ?

The salary is $2,500 a year. There has been no change in his salary since he was appointed. His duties are to supervise the work of the forestry branch which is divided into two classes. One class of the work consists in the preparation of material for tree planting; that is to say young trees delivered to farmers in different parts of the prairie country are planted under the supervision of the inspectors or supervisors appointed for that purpose. The other division of the work consists in taking such steps as may be found practicable for the purpose of preventing the origination and spread of fires. I may say that this is a class of work which might be with great advantage considerably extended and the reason why it is not considerably extended is due to the fact that we do not feel like asking for a larger appropriation. Hon. gentlemen will see that $10,000 out of the $25,000 we are asking for is for the payment of fire rangers in different sections of the country. I am told that last year the work of the fire rangers appointed by this branch of the service saved very large quantities of timber which unquestionably would otherwise have been destroyed, and I fancy there is no vote in connection with the service of the Department of the Interior which more fully justifies itself in the saving of property which forms part of the public domain.
What portion of the vote is for tree culture and how is it to be spent ? I did not have the opportunity of being at the Agriculture Committee.

$10,000 is for the salaries of fire rangers

and there will be, perhaps, $2,000 or $3,000 additional out of the $25,000 spent in other ways in connection with the prevention of fires. About half of the vote will be applicable to the work of the preparation and the planting of trees.
Will the hon. minister tell us the modus operandi in regard to the growth and distribution of trees? Do you furnish trees free to the farmers ?

We have plantations upon the Experimental Farms at Brandon and Indian Head where large quantities of young trees are grown to an age- suitable for transplanting. These young trees are handed over to farmers who apply for them and who agree to plant them under the directions which are furnished by the forestry branch and under the supervision of the officers appointed for that purpose. During this spring over a million young trefes were delivered to those who applied for them.
When Mr. Stewart was before the committee he admitted that at the rate these trees were being given out it would take a long time to re-forest the North-west.
It is a large country.

Mr. Stewart tacitly agreed that trees selected from a bluff adjoining a man's home would answer the purpose as well as the present system. I would suggest to the minister that the fire law in relation to the burning of scrub timber lands might very well be inquired into. In Assiniboia and the southern part of Alberta, only possibly the southern part of Saskatchewan, apparently the present fire law is very proper, but in the northern part of these territories it would be a great blessing if a good fire would sweep over the country and burn the underbrush which varies in size and density and which has to be cleared by the settler with even greater labour than confronted the early pioneers of Ontario in clearing the forests. I would suggest that the minister might inquire whether the regulations may not be amended in relation to the fall fires in the extreme northern part of Alberta and Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I would suggest to the minister the advisability of trying to grow hickory trees in the North-west. It is a timber which is very largely used in Canada now and the supply has become almost entirely exhausted.

The trees best adapted for the North-west are the soft wood trees, such as cotton wood, poplar and Manitoba maple, which grow well and are excellent shade trees. I think it would be useless to try to get hickory to grow.
I was somewhat astonished to hear the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) asking that the regulations respecting prairie fires in northern Alberta should be relaxed.
Not prairie fires; wood fires.

Well wood or prairie fires, because if a fire spreads in the prairie it does not stop when it gets to the wood. I do not know how far the hon. gentleman's suggestion is likely to be acted upon by the minister, but having been a member of the North-west Assembly for a number of years, I can say to the House that the question of preventing as far as possible fires of all kinds from running in any part of the country and particularly in the wooded and partly wooded parts of the country, is a subject that has occupied the attention of the North-west Assembly ever since I have known anything about it. If the wood is small or if it is scarce it is all the more necessary that it should not be dsetroyed by prairie fires. If there should be regulations as there are for the preservation of the wood so that it shall not be cut wastefully by settlers, surely it is a thousand times more necessary that it should not be destroyed by uncontrolled fires. I do not wish to engage in a controversy at this particular stage of the game, but I cannot allow the suggestion to pass without a most emphatic protest and to say to the minister as representing that part of the country, that I

would most strongly urge not only that tlie present restrictions be maintained-of course he has no control over them-but that the present means of maintaining these restrictions over which he has control be rather improved and enlarged than otherwise.
The MINISTER OF THE( INTERIOR. In reply to my hon. friend, I have now before me the report. It was written in August of last year, and refers to the work of the spring of 1902 :
This spring ninety-one applicants were supplied with trees from Indian Head, the total number of seedings and cuttings sent out being 106,000, consisting of 33,256 maples, 53,648 cottonwoods, 2,000 elm and 17,096 willow cuttings.
The following is an estimate of stock at present growing in the Indian Head nursery :-

Elm	 50,000
Scotch pine, one year old	 25,000

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Allow me to suggest to the minister that he recommend to the gentleman in charge at Indian Head that he try some of the other hardwood timber. Where ash and elm will grow hickory will grow, and it is one of the most valuable timbers, and one of the quickest growers. We are to-day importing into Canada very large quantities of hickory from the United States. We cannot get it anywhere else, the supply in Canada being exhausted. If the department could make a success of growing hickory, nothing more valuable to the country could happen than to plant some of those untold acres in the North-west with hickory trees. In twenty years from now we would have a supply for the manufacturers of this country, and save importing it from a foreign country. It would be worth trying at any rate, to see whether or not it would be a success.

I am glad to have this suggestion from my hon. friend, who has a practical knowledge of woods required for manufacturing purposes. I have a strong idea of the value of this work, if the farmers of the country could be induced to take it up. The amount we can do ourselves is of course comparatively small; but if we can induce the farmers of the country, who have unlimited ground, to engage in tree planting, and to plant that class of trees which will be economically valuable, I am satisfied that we shall accomplish a great thing for the country. I am glad to have my hon. friend's suggestion, and I will see that it receives full consideration.

I do not like to run foul of my hon. friend from Alberta (Mr. Oliver), but I wish to say that what I had reference to was not timber land,
but land covered with scrub. Wherever you find a clump of scrub, you invariably have early frosts in the fall and late frosts in the spring; and many of the settlers in northern Saskatchewan and in many parts of northern Alberta would be delighted if some relaxation in the restrictions with regard to fall fires might be allowed, so that they might get the land cleared of scrub, and relieved of the dampness and consequently of the early fall frosts which are caused thereby. I believe in preserving the timber lands at every cost; but this scrub is absolutely useless for fuel, and it is an almost impossible job for the farmers to get rid of it.
What limitations are there with regard to giving out these seedlings ? Can any person anywhere in the North-west or in Manitoba get all he wants ?

Yes. The trouble has been to induce the farmers to take them at all, and look after them. Of course, if the demand became large, the agent would exercise his discretion and not give a larger number to one man than he could look after.

I quite appreciate the advantage of giving them out as an object lesson, to induce the farmers to purchase them in the future; but I would suggest that there should be ultimately some restriction imposed. I imagine that when the farmers of the North-west find that they can get these seedlings free and in unlimited numbers, in a short time there will be such an enormous demand for them, that it will be a great tax on the government to supply them. It seems to me, too, that it is rather unfair that the farmers of one section are furnished with these seedlings free, while the farmers of another section are not. In the United States, the government for a time sent out free seeds. At first there was not much demand for them; but presently the giving out of free seeds not only became a great burden on the government, but an intolerable nuisance.

If a general demand arose, the natural result would be that people would go into the nursery business on a large scale; and as soon as that cbndition of affairs arose, the government would cease to supply the trees, and leave the work to private enterprise.

A year or two ago, Mr. Stewart, before the Committee on Agriculture, said that if any person wanted trees to plant and made application for them, the government would send a person to look at his farm and prescribe the kind of trees that would be best suited to it, and would lay out a diagram in a rough way as to how they should be planted. That diagram would be sent to Ottawa, and in

the following year the inspector would go out and see what had been done. I would like to know if that plan has been carried out ?
I think, generally speaking, it has. I would not say that there are no exceptions.
Is not that a very expensive modus operandi ?

Of course, it is expensive. The expenses consist in sending a man out to see that the planting is properly done. There are scores of cases where farmers have tried to plant trees in absolute ignorance of the methods that ought to be adopted ; and after a few years, some of these trees are half dead and others completely withered. The principle of this has been to furnish an object lesson and that is necessarily expensive.

I could quite understand this being done in districts, but Mr. Stewart left the impression on the minds of the committee that if any one applied, an inspector would be sent down to view his soil, make a rough diagram, send that to Ottawa and get a regular plan made, then plant the trees, and the following year inspect them.

1 do not think the intention was to send an inspector out to make a diagram before any trees were planted, but that a diagram would be sent showing how the trees should be planted, and then the inspector would be sent to supervise the planting.
I suppose your travelling foresters are paid their actual expenses 7
There is nothing paid except the actual expenses, for which vouchers are furnished.

I see an item here of a pullman and state-room for Mr. Stewart, $131.25. Of course, these gentlemen must travel in state as much as possible, and I presume these things are not put down at lower than cost. There is another item of $839.49 for printing in connection with Dominion lands, protection of timber.
We have to get notices printed showing what the law is with regard tp allowing fires to run, and these notices have to be printed on a special kind of paper, and are rather expensive.
Where are they printed ?
At the Printing Bureau.
When did the department begin giving out the trees referred to, and to what extent have the farmers taken advantage of that policy ?

My recollection is that three years ago we Mr. WILSON.
started with our first vote of $15,000, and the vote has been $15,000 per year since then. I do not think I could give a better idea of the result of the work than will be found on page 10 of the Report of the Department of the Interior.

I think that Mr. Stewart made the statement before the committee that it was almost impossible for the department to furnish sufficient trees to supply the demands of the farmers ; but if I understood the hon. minister, the difficulty with the department was to get the farmers to plant the trees.

My hon. friend may have referred to the difficulty experienced at first. It was only towards the end of the second year that we decided upon fitting out these plantations. I am informed that the supply is equal to the demand, but no doubt the demand will grow rapidly.
Is a man sent out to show farmers how to plant the trees and lay out the ground ?
That rule is not always followed. Where the farmer knows sufficient himself, we do not send any one to teach him.
Suppose an inquiry came 200 miles distant, would the minister send a man that distance ?
The applications would come in early in the season, and the superintendent would de-vide his staff and use his judgment as to where he would send them.
As there are only two centres, there might be some points many hundreds of miles away from them, and it would be an expensive job.
In that case we cannot do it.

Printed instructions might be sent out which woujd be quite sufficient. That is all the farmers in the east require. With such instructions, it is not more difficult to plant small seedlings than any farm crop.

It appears to me a pretty expensive job. I do not know why the farmers in Manitoba and the Northwest should not be able to plant seedling trees. In our section of the country we buy our apple trees, at pretty high prices too, and we have no government official running around to tell us how to plant our trees. A man who is capable of running a farm ought to have intelligence enough to plant trees. In addition, we have an inspector, if what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) says is correct, travelling about superintending this work, and he travels in a pullman car.
With a state-room.

Of course. And we do not hear anything from the supporters of the government about it. But I can remember the time when, if one of the members of the government I had the honour to support travelled in a pullman car, the fact was heralded from one end of the country to the other, and one would have thought that these lion, gentlemen on the other side would lose their senses at such an extravagance perpetrated by a member of the government. Even the cab-hire of the leader of the government, Sir John A. Macdonald, was criticised. And now the inspector wh i is to teach the farmers of the North-west to plant trees is not satisfied with travelling like an ordinary mortal, but he must have a pullman car and a state-room.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) seems to think it peculiar that this work is carried on in Manitoba and the North-west, and in no other province V
No, I do not.
That is what I gather from his remarks. He said that the farmers in his part of the country had to buy their own trees at pretty high prices-
I said that they bought trees that were expensive, and they did not have a government official running around to tell them how to plant them.
The hon. gentleman says the farmers in his section buy their own trees, and the inference, as I suppose, is that the farmers in the North-west ought to buy theirs.
I did not say so.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) was referring to the planting of the trees and the intelligence required in that work.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will permit me-I would like to point out that the conditions in the Northwest are not similar to those in the older provinces. The Dominion government owns all the public lands in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and it does not own the public lands in the other parts of Canada. That is a reason why, if this work is done for the preservation of forests and the encouragement of tree planting, it should be done by the authority and at the expense of the Dominion government.
Are these trees being planted upon public lands ?

A part of this expenditure is upon government lands for the preservation of the forest. What I rose for chiefly was to protest against the useless waste of time in asking questions such as have been | asked this evening, the answers to which 1
would be known to hon. gentlemen if they would take the trouble to read the report of the superintendent of forestry. I have here that report for 1902, which gives specifically the answers to many of the questions that have been asked with regard to the carrying on of the work. For instance, as to whether the department is going to be able [DOT]to supply the demands which come from the people for trees. At page eight of the report I find the following :
In the spring of 1901 a beginning was made by furnishing forty-four settlers, who had their ground prepared, with seedling trees. In all 58,800 trees were sent out at that time.
In the spring of 1902, 415 settlers were supplied, the aggregate quantity being 468,900 trees	There are in all 1,006 applicants whose land is being examined . this season with a view to planting next spring.
Applications are now being received from those who desire to have their places examined next season with a view to making preparation for receiving trees for planting in 1904. . . .
The matter of being able to supply the applicants with seedling trees has been one of some concern, and fears were expressed that it might, be impossible to meet the large demands that would be made. I am glad, however. to be able to report that the nurseries established by this department at the Experimental Farms at Brandon and Indian Head through the kind permission of the minister and officers of the Department of Agriculture, will furnish over 1,000,000 trees for transplanting next spring. In addition to these we will probably have 150,000 maples and Russian poplars from Mr. Caldwell, at Virden. So it may be safely assumed that all applicants who have their ground properly prepared for next spring's planting will receive their full complement of nursery stock.
There Is a complete answer from the report to several of the questions that have been asked ; and I venture to say that the report contains specific information, answering practically every question With which the time of the committee has been taken up this evening.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) will allow a question, as he seems so conversant with these points ? Perhaps he can tell us what portion of the money has been spent on private property, and what on public property in respect to the planting of trees ?

I have to admit I am not very conversant with these matters, and cannot answer the question. But I have no doubt the hon. gentleman will be able to obtain an answer from the minister. My principal objection to this vote is that not enough money is being spent upon this object. I consider It, and it is considered by all the peole of Manitoba and the Northwest, as one of the most important objects with which this parliament has to deal affecting that part of the country. The pity is that practical work was not begun sooner. This is not a new subject, and the present plan is much more economical and effective,

in my opinion, than that followed by the late government in years gone by. For this is a subject that did not entirely escape their attention. They endeavoured to encourage tree planting by allowing men to gain the title to their homesteads and also to the pre-emption of an additional 160 acres, which, in former years they were allowed to obtain. That plan was much more expensive than the practical and effective plan adopted by the present Minister of the Interior.

The House, I am sure, is muqh delighted with the information obtained from the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott). It appears to me that he wishes to be a second epistle of the Minister of the Interior. I suppose he is moved by the legitimate ambition of at one time filling the position of Minister of the Interior. The hon. gentleman was good enough to criticise the opposition for occupying the time of the House. I am within the judgment of the House when I say that the hon. gentleman has occupied more than his share of time in elaborating his views and giving us information that amounts to nothing when he gets through with it. He must be well satisfied with himself, and I am sure the Minister of the Interior is delighted that there is a second epistle to himself in this House ready to afford us information whether he has it or not. I did not offer the criticism that the hon. gentleman thought I did. He must not put words in my mouth that I never used. I did not object to the country spending money in furnishing trees, what I objected to was sending out officials to tell the farmers bow to plant the trees, and I referred to tli? fact that in Ontario we have to plant our own fruit trees, that cost us a good deal of inoney. I do not see why the farmer in the North-west, if he has brains enough to farm, should not have brains enough to set out a few trees when they are furnished him by the government. I object to the unnecessary expenditure of this gentleman travelling in pullman cars. I find in looking over the Auditor General's Report that there is one gentleman who has got a ' span of ponies. I would ask the second epistle of the Minister of the Interior whether it is shown in that report that some gentleman has got a span of ponies at $225. He is not only travelling in state in the pullman car, and state-rooms, but he has got a span of ponies that cost the country $225. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if I could find that in this report. I think the whole thing is absurd, and when people will read it they will fay, great Scott, what is this country coming to ?
If the hon. gentleman wants information about a span of ponies and thinks there is anything wrong in this officer having a span of ponies, we have the

Public Accounts Committee and other committees who are appointed to deal with such questions. Surely the time of this House should not be taken up with discussing questions of no more importance than this.
I protest against the way in which, for the past three months, the time of this House has been recklessly wasted by hon. gentlemen day after day and night after nigut. One night we were kept in session until nearly half past seven o'clock in the morning, and,what was the discussion about ? The list of questions in the census schedules which I presume every person in Canada had already seen. I protest against hon. gentlemen wasting the time of the House in such manner.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I rise to a point of order. The hon. gentleman is not talking to the question before the Chair. He is accusing hon. gentlemen of obstructing. I do not know of any person who is doing it more effectively than he is doing it himself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think there are quite a number who are not speaking to the resolution, and I would advise hon. gentlemen to get back and discuss the merits of this item. I appeal to them all to keep a little closer to the question under consideration.

The only difference between the other side of the House and this side is upon the question whether the public money should be expended on private property. Our side of the House do not make any complaint against an expenditure of government money to supply trees to farmers in the western country ; but what we 'say is that it is not proper that the government should expend money in sending out an official to examine the land, and then sending him out again to help plant the trees in order to beautify a farmer's property. I may say to the hon. gentleman that when Mr. Stewart was before the committee he submitted a plan and distributed it among members of the committee, showing the different ways in wRich different properties should be' laid out. That gentleman told the committee that when a farmer made application for trees, the department sent a man out to find out what kind of land he proposed to plant the trees upon. That was the first expense, and that is something we object to. After he had found out what kind of land the farmer had, and what kind of soil, the department then sent him out to assist in laying out that property and in planting the trees. That is an expenditure-that we are objecting to. We know that in that country it is not easy to grow trees, and we do not at all object to the government supplying the trees. We would go so far as to say that when farmers apply for trees the government should keep-an abundant supply on hand so as to furnish every farmer who applies for them. But what'we do object to is in the governt>7 85

ment, first of all, sending officials out to inspect iiie property, and after supplying the trees, to assist the farmer in beautifying his property, a private property which ought not to be improved by public money.

I do not think the hon. gentleman seriously objects to this item. I mav say that tree planting in the North-west was practically unknown a short time ago. The system has undergone a considerable amount of improvement, and we have reason to hope that by following out the plan we are at present pursuing the result will be to encourage tree planting to a considerable extent throughout that country. Generally speaking, the principle of expending public money on private properties is, of course, indefensible, but the hon. gentleman will understand that this is done only temporarily and to a small extent.

I took the same ground before the committee when Mr. Stewart was before us that I do now. I do not object to the government giving the trees, but I think it is altogether too much to send a man out to inspect the ground, to make a diagram of it. to send the diagram to Ottawa, and have the plan sent back, and then after the trees are planted to send a man out again to inspect them. I objected to that then, and I object to it now.

I notice in the Auditor General's Report, L

91, an item for 300.000 cottonwood trees at $375. Do you buy your cottonwood trees in the western states ?
The MINISTER OF THE INi . .	.
These were bought in Dakota. We are raising some now.
Can you not get these trees in Canada ?

I do not think we can get cottonwood trees in Canada. Some of our nurserymen in the North-west say that only cottonwood trees grow well on our prairies. I remember the question was discussed when the Minister of Agriculture introduced legislation to prevent the importation of trees from the United States, on account of the prevalence of the San Jose scale. My recollection is that the nurserymen of Manitoba were of the opinion that the only cottonwood tree that could be got to grow in the North-west was that which came from North Dakota.

The cottonwood tree is raised here as well as in Dakota. The only question is as to whether or not it has been grown here. If the department is going to continue the planting of these trees I would suggest that an arrangement be made to grow them in Canada.

They will grow just as well in the nurseries 213
of Manitoba and the North-west Territories as in Dakota. I am not able to say why it is they have not planted cottonwood on the farms.
I notice in these items money paid out for the purchase of horses and in connection with trading horses. I do not see any credit showing what has been done with these animals.
What page ?

Page L-90, under Dominion Lands.
Team of pony mares, $225 ; team harness, half set, $15 ; freight, $91.19 ; single harness, $35 ; curry comb, brush, &c., $1.35.
In another place I find
Lodging and horse feed, $375.15 ; fountain pen, $4.50 ; fountain pen, $3.
They seem to be supplied with everything. What is done with these horses ? Do they give them away when they are through with them ?
These items are for horse hire, I suppose.
This is for the purchase of horses and trading horses.
Mr. Ross, the assistant superintendent, has a horse and Mr. Stevenson has a horse. The others all hire horses where they are required.
What was Mr. Ross' business before he undertook the work of superintendent of tree planting ? I understand he was just a farmer who had lived in that country for a while ?
Mr. Ross is a gentleman who had previously devoted himself before coming into the department to the study of forestry. He has a special education on these lines.
Where did he live ?

My recollection is that immediately previous to his coming into the service of the department he was at Toronto. I cannot at this moment give the record, but Mr. Ross devoted himself especially to the study of forestry. He had studied it under specialists in Europe, having gone there for the purpose, as a scientific education in forestry cannot be procured on this continent. After having spent some time in Europe, Mr. Ross returned and continued his studies under Dr. Schenck, one of the most eminent foresters in the world, who is in charge of the Vanderbilt estate in South Carolina.
What is his salary 1
That is not very high for so highly educated a man.
Talking about horses, here is one item.

services, October 15 to December 31. at $75. $191.13 ; board, lodging and horse teed, $93.50 ; horse-hire, 1105.50 ; fares, $7.80. $397.93.
I do not know whether these horses are owned or not, but in several instances throughout this report-not in connection with this service-horses are bought and traded and so much given in trade, $15 in one place and $35 in another place. Then, there is ' horseshoeing, $2.70.' and another item ' shoeing horses, $3.75.' Take a case like this.
Wodrow, W. A.: horse-hire, $105.50-
and
-'lodging and horse feed, $93.50.
That is $198 for two and a half months. It seems to me to be an awful figure.

Mr. Woodrow is a nurseryman. He had $75 a month while he was working and we paid his expenses while he was travelling in the service of the department from October 15 to December 31. During that time he paid $105 for horse-hire. If my hon. friend was travelling through the country and had to hire horses he would have to pay that much. I know I would; in fact I generally have to pay more. 1 do not think the amount is excessive.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Carried.

Before we pass to the next item the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) asked me before six o'clock to give an approximate statement of the amount of land that is available in the organized portions of the North-west Territories for settlement. I want to guard myself in making this statement because it would be difficult except after a very elaborate and careful calculation, to give a statement that could be regarded as accurate. I can only give a very rough approximate statement, but still, even speaking in that sense, one which I think will be of some value to the members of the committee. The total area of land in the organized districts of the Northwest Territories is 230.000,000 acres. There have been disposed of in homesteads and pre-emptions, roughly speaking, about 18,000,000 acres, and there have been given to railway companies, colonization companies, &c., by way of grants of one kind or another 58,000,000 acres. That leaves a balance of 154,000,000 acres. I would deduct from that 54,000,000 acres of land that is not fairly fit for settlement, either land which is covered with water or of a rough and broken character; so that, roughly speaking, we have 100,000,000 acres of land still available for settlement in the organized territories.
What do you mean by organized territories ?

I mean the territories which have been by Act of this parliament organized into districts-Manitoba, Eastern Assiniboia, Western Assiniboia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan. North of that country we have the unorganized districts of Athabasca and Mackenzie.
Military asylum pensions, $168.

I have the explanation of this vote here, and I wish to mention it, so when it comes up in connection with some other department the explanation will have been given. This is a small item but sometimes questions are asked about it. It is made up of three or four small pensions which are provided for by 44 Victoria, chapter 18.
Maintenance, construction of roads, bridges and other necessary works in connection with the Hot Springs reservation near Banff station, Northrwest Territories, $22,420.
How much money was spent out of the vote last year ?
It was all spent.
Can you give us the items of expenditure last year ?
I have not the return showing how the money was actually spent.
How much money has been spent on that park up to date ?
I cannot say.
How many acres in it

It is in the form of a triangle, the side on the British Columbia boundary being about 130 miles and the other about 115 miles long. We have added what is called the Yoho park which is in British Columbia and although technically not a part of the same park it is under the same administration. We own the land and have the sovereign right in the North-west Territories, but that part on the British Columbia side is held by the federal government as private owners of property in the province. The universal report is that the park is a source of great pleasure to travellers. The number of visitors has greatly increased, and when I was there, in the month of December, a year and a half ago, I was told that the hotels had been so filled at the close of the season that they had to send word ahead that they could not accommodate any m re visitors. The Canadian Pacific Railway has since increased its hotel accommodation, and last year we erected a museum and office where visitors may gather and obtain information. There are over 100 miles of

constructed roads in the park; we have 36 or 37 buffalo, and they are being successfully bred ; we have a small herd of elk and of moose. It is our intention to have a collection of animals there. The superintendent of the park is a very efficient officer, and I think we get very good value for what money we spend.
How will the appropriation of $3,000 for the baths be expended ?

One of the attractions of the park is the medicinal springs which are very curative in rheumatic diseases. A small fee is charged to the visitors for the use of the bathing house, and these fees pay the superintendence of the bath to a considerable extent. It is proposed on account of the increasing number of visitors to increase the bath house accommodation.

I must congratulate the minister on the expenditure. I can assure him that, if it is properly spent, it is well needed. The old bath-house was rather a disgrace to the country, and I am very glad to know that the minister has put a small sum in the estimates to improve it.
Will the minister say who the caretaker is, and how many employees there are at Banff Springs ?

There are four regular employees :	Mr. Howard Douglas, superintendent ; Mr. Ellis, caretaker of buffalo ; Mr. Galletly, caretaker of cave and basin ; and Mr. Sanson, curator of the museum at the office building. Any other persons whose names appear in the Auditor General's Report are paid in a temporary way. They are not permanent officials.

I understand that there is a splendid hotel at Banff run by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and that there are baths in connection with that hotel. The question is why we should keep public baths there instead of leaving that entirely to private enterprise. There may be some reasoti that I do not know, but I have not heard any yet.

The baths of the Canadian Pacific Railway hotel are for the guests of the hotel. The baths of the department are patronized by a great many people who do not care to go to the expense of stopping at the hotel. As a matter of fact, the greater number of patients who go there for treatment take up their residences at cottages in the neighbourhood, where the expense is not so great as at the hotel, and they make use of the government baths, which are intended for the use of the public generally.
Construction of roads, bridle paths and other necessary works in connection with the Yoho Park reserve, $10,000.

The Yoho park is in the same valley as that portion of the Banff park where the buildings are and through which the railway runs. It is practically a continuation of the Banff park. I may say that in that park there have been discovered very considerable natural beauties, the presence of which had not been suspected until the last year or two. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company went to considerable expense in bringing over Alpine mountain climbers to make explorations, with the result that very large glaciers were discovered in the vicinity of the railway track. They will form a great attraction to the park, though quite inaccessible except to mountain climbers. We are taking steps to construct roads and bridle paths to make these natural beauties accessible.
The minister appears to have a herd of buffalo in the park, I believe the only herd that there is in North America. Is it increasing ?

Yes, very satisfactorily. We are quite satisfied with the experiment we have made. We started with a herd of about 19, and we have now 35 or 36. At some places, of course, the buffalo will not thrive, and it was more or less of an experiment to take these to the Banff park. We got sixteen or seventeen head from Lord Strathcona. They had been at Silver Heights, near the city of Winnipeg, but they had not done well there. We also got three head from Mr. Thomas Blackstock, of Toronto, who contributed them on my promise to attempt to establish a herd. We established the herd, and provided a large enclosure for them, and they have been thriving and doing very well.

Is this the work of the delimiting of the boundaries ?

Yes, the 49th parallel.

Carried on in connection with the officers of the United States government ?

Yes.

How much work have you got done ? Mr. King has been there some years at work. What distance of delimitation have you accomplished ?
