Astronomical observatory for telescope and apparatus, $5,000.

Is that the observatory you are building here ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Yes, on the Experimental Farm. We had a great deal of trouble finding a suitable site. It was difficult to get a site sufficiently elevated, so that the view from the tower would not be obstructed. Other considerations also had to be taken into account.
The site had to be a place where the oscillation caused by railway currents would not affect the setting of the instruments.
The railways pass close to the Experimental Farm.
Quite far enough away not to have any effect.
There is a good deal of discussion in the press about your moving the observatory from Toronto.
That is the meteorological survey, which is under the Marine Department.
Has a telescope been bought, and at what price 7
Yes ; about $15,000.
What is the diameter of your lens and the power of your instrument ?
My impression is that it is a 12-inch lens.
That would be very small.
I relied upon the chief astronomer.

It could not be very strong with only a 12-inch 'lens. It is not the height of wisdom to put up some commonplace telescope, because it must remain there a credit to the government or otherwise ; and before you could change it, you would have to remodel the building.
THE MINISTER OF THE [DOT] INTERIOR. I told the chief astronomer that I thought it would be false economy to buy an instrument which would have to be changed, and impressed upon him the selection of an instrument which would not be required to be changed.
Where was the telescope purchased ?
In Cleveland. In our chief astronomer we have a very able officer. He started as Dominion land surveyor in 1873 or 1874.
Was he attending to the boundary survey ?

He was British commissioner under the treaty of 1892. He is now in England, and will be there until the argument in connection with the Alaskan boundary is over. He is an expert officer and thoroughly posted. His presence there is necessary. I was remarking to the committee that in Mr. King we have one of the ablest and most competent officers of the government. I have no doubt that his judgment with respect to the apparatus is perfectly good.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: No doubt it is; lie is a good man. How much is it expected the observatory will cost when completed ? What has been done besides purchasing the instrument ?

The building is under the Department of Public Works, and I have nothing to do with it. We took a vote last year for the purchase of the instruments. We have done nothing of any account in this respect, except the purchase of the telescope, which cost $15,000. This is a vote of $5,000 for miscellaneous apparatus.
When does tlie hon. minister expect that the observatory will be finished 7

I cannot say. I have been pressing upon the Department of Public Works the necessity of proceeding with all despatch. Since coming back from England, I have not had time to make inquiries about the matter, but I believe the work is progressing. I have no doubt it will be finished within a few months.

I have been credibly informed that the building will not be finished within two years. The foundation has been laid, but it will be a somewhat expensive building. The hon. minister says the telescope was bought a year ago and $15,000 paid for it. What kind of political economy, or any other economy, does he call this-paying $15,000 for a telescope three years before it is wanted ?

I can only say that the order for the telescope was given a year and a half ago, and my deputy tells me that it has lately arrived. If the building has not arrived at the same time, I am not directly responsible. The Department of Public Works have received their instructions, and I can only hope the building will be finished as soon as possible. Had we waited until the building was up before ordering the telescope we might have had the building a year or two ahead of the telescope.
I see by the newspapers that the observatory is to remain in Toronto.
That is the meteorological observatory.
The telescope will cost $1,800 in interest before it is brought into use-three years' interest on $15,000 at four per cent.
That is one of the difficulties arising through not having everything under one department.
Does this complete the cost of equipping the observatory 7

I think so. I had a discussion in England with the astronomer with regard to this particular Item, and this vote will be sufficient. Of course, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will understand that an observatory or a laboratory is never completed. A scientific man can always find something more that he wants. But, for the present, this is enough.
It will equip it completely until the next vote 7
Yes.
I do not know whether the hon. minister answered my question as to the total cost jof the building and equipment.
I can only say that the contract for the building was $75,000, speaking from recollection. There was a vote of $15,000 last year for the equipment, and $5,000 now, making $20,000 for the equipment.

That makes a total of
about $100,000. Did I understand the hon. minister to say anything about a laboratory in connection with this establishment 7

No, I only made the remark that when a scientific man has a laboratory or observatory he can always find something more that he wants for its equipment, therefore, I would not say that the observatory would be completely equipped with this amount.
On the subject of meteorological reports, has the hon. minister taken any steps to extend the collection of these reports so as to include the remote parts of the North-west and British Columbia 7

I have nothing to do with the meteorological service, that is under the direction of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.
Miscellaneous-'costs of litigation, $11,000.
I notice that a similar amount to this was voted last year. How much of it was spent 7

The report of last year has not been made up. In the year previous, we spent $1,938. \Ve have a number of cases coming up this year, which will involve a considerable amount of expenditure for legal fees, and I presume the Department of Justice will require the Department of the Interior to pay the Bills after they are taxed, and we shall perhaps spend $10,000 or $11,000.

I regard it as a bad plan to provide a lot of money for litigation. In almost every department a large sum is voted for this purpose. If you put it there

it is almost sure to be spent. We have a Department of Justice with a pretty large staff, and one would naturally suppose that they would attend to a good deal of the work required to be done, but the amount placed at the disposal of each of the departments is almost sure to be distributed amongst the lawyers or hangers-on of the government.

What my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) says, is generally speaking, perfectly true. If you put a sum of money to the credit of the service, the tendency is for them to spend it. But in this case, the amount voted really has no effect upon the amount actually expended. When this litigation arises, the costs of the litigation, if they are payable by the government, are taxed by the Department of Justice, and we have to pay them. When the Bill becomes due we wait till the end of the fiscal year and take an estimate for it.
We are asked to pay this money, and we have no information regarding the services performed. It seems to me that there is a large amount of money paid out for very little work.

My hon. friend will have to talk with the Minister of Justice about that, because that does not belong to my department. The present item is merely for the purpose of paying legal expenses in suits arising in matters belonging to the business of the Department of the Interior. The expenses have to be certified by the Department of Justice. If anybody brings a suit in which the Department of the Interior is defendant. if there are any law costs payable, we have to pay them. The litigation is conducted by the Department of Justice and the costs are certified by the Department of Justice. I understand the rule is that we do not require to pay the eosts of the opposing party, but we have to pay our own costs.
On page L-50, I see an item ' Amount paid to F. W. Howie, New Westminster, $1,000.' What is the explanation of that item ?

A dispute arose in British Columbia in regard to some timber land. A man named Genelle sued the Crown for damages, and the amount mentioned here, $1,000, was paid to the Justice Department for Mr. Howie, to meet the disbursements in connection with witnesses, fees and expenses.
I do not know whether the suit has terminated yet. My recollection is that it has not yet been brought to trial. We have been advised that we have a good case.

Would the minister give us some details of this sum of $1,000 ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR, It is money that was paid by the Justice ^ Mr. SPROULE.
Department to their agent at New Westminster to pay for his services in connection with this suit. I suppose the Department of Justice will sooner or later have the details. If the details have come back and been returned to the Auditor General's office they will appear in his report. When the vouchers come back the items will appear in the Auditor General's Report.

Was Mr. Howie your solicitor in New Westminster -who attended to the case ?
The MINiSTER OF THE INTERIOR. I presume he is the agent of the Department of Justice. The litigation is conducted by the Department of Justice.
There must be vouchers of some kind for this expenditure.

; There will be of course. When the department pays the money we are required to tile a detailed statement with the Auditor General, accounting for that money. If the department lets it go for a certain length of time and the Auditor General thinks it is an unreasonable time, he calls upon us to account for that money.

That does not enable us to get any information. We apply to the Minister of the Interior and he refers us to the Minister of Justice or to the Auditor General. We want some details of what was paid. We have no information of what the disbursements were.

The reason why the details are not given is because the action has not arrived at that stage when the Auditor General requires this money to be accounted for. If it is desired to get them before the matter reaches that stage, the only way will be, if a report has not yet been received from Mr. Howie, to get the Department of Justice tq write' to him for it.

The Auditor General's Report is over a year old. surely by tnis time somebody' must have the vouchers. They must be in the possession of some department, otherwise the business must be done in a remarkably loose way.

Not only that, but even in this ancient document, the Auditor General's Report for 1902, there is an expenditure of $1,000. Now we are asked to vote $11,000. It seems to me we ought to have every detail of such a large vote, especially when it is for litigation.
If the hon. gentleman wishes to have a list of the suits which are pending, I have not got them in my hands, but I will get them to-morrow.
Are there several suits or .just one 7
There are several. Some I know of myself. I cannot remember, speaking from memory, all of them.
In the Auditor General's Report for 1902 we only seem to have paid $1,000 for the case of Genelle vs. the King.
There have been several suits within the last year.
I am afraid of the devil's claw.

There are three in connection with Dominion lands and one or two that came from the Yukon. If the hon. gentleman desires it I will give him a list of them. I cannot do it now because I do not have it amongst my papers.
Expenses of government in district of Kee-watin, $2,190.
What do you spend this for ?

As my hon. friend knows the lieutenant governor of Keewatin is the lieutenant governor of Manitoba. He holds that additional office. He has a private secretary with an allowance of $600, and a clerk with an allowance of $480.
What duties does the lieutenant governor perform ?

He is supposed to inform himself generally as to what is going on in that territory. The territory is practically uninhabited except for the presence of 200 Indians in it. It is necessary to have some supervision over it and the practice that has been followed for many years has been that the lieutenant governor of Manitoba has been appointed for that purpose. He has to make one trip every year and he makes a report to the government as to what is going on in that section of the country. There are many matters that require the attention of the government.
Is there any such report in the possession of the government now ?
It will be found in the report of my department.

I have been told that some lieutenant governors do not visit the territory at all. but that they get the money all the same. Is there any information to that effect in the possession of the hon. minister ?

I do not remember whether he went last year or not, but I know he went the year before. I remember reading the report
carefully at the time it came in. He says in his last report:-
In making my annual report upon affairs in the district of Keewatin during the past year,
I am glad to be able to say that no occurrence calling for special notice has taken place during the year. Circumstances have prevented my paying an extended visit through the district.
I have, however, come into communication with and met some of the missionaries, the principal Hudson's Bay Company's officers and others who carry on trade in the territory, and have thus kept in comparatively close touch and been made well acquainted with the condition of the native population during the past year.
How much of the vote did he use up last year-the whole of it ?
How did he expend that amount if he did not go there ?

The amount is made up in this way :-
One clerk, $4S0 ; salary of secretary, $600 ; department printing and stationery, Ottawa, printing, &c., $23.22.
That is all of the expenditure.

It seems to me that it would be better if this money is employed, properly no doubt, in paying the secretary of the governor that we should say so.
Expenses of government in district of Kee-aatin.
There are no expenses there. It is S600 for a secretary and $480 for smnp one else and $23 for stationery. Would it not be better to put it in the vote in that way ? I appeal to you, Mr. Chairman. What is the use of dissimulating and why should we vote $2,190 to cover expenses which last year amounted to $1,103 ? It is not much, but it is for the principle that we are combating.
Maintenance of lunatics from Keewatin, *2,000.
I thought you had nothing there but a few Indians. Where do you get the lunatics from ?
Indians occasionally go crazy and we have to take care of them.
How many are there in the asylum and where are they kept ? Are they kept at Brandon too ?
Last year we paid $744.10 to the Brandon asylum for the maintenance of three lunatics.	.
How did you come to know there were any out there if nobody ever visits the district ?

The year before last the lieutenant governor did visit it. The lieutenant governor exer-

cises a general supervision. He gets information from traders from the Hudson's Bay Company, and from clergymen as to what is going on. If he hears of any lunatics they are brought down.
Maintenance of assay office at Vancouver, $17)0Q0.
This vote is for the salaries and expenses in connection with the assay office at Vancouver.
Have you any report of the work done during the past year ?
The work is somewhat less now than it was, on account of the change in the mode of collecting the royalty. Full details are given in part 6 of the annual report of the department.
What revenue was received from the office ?

There is no statement which shows a revenue under the operations of last year. The method of computation is very complicated. Tli? principle upon which we established the office was not to make any charge for the work done, because we wanted to secure the business in Canada rather than have it to go to Seattle.
Do you not make any charge at all ?
Not last year, but I understand the superintendent is making a small charge this year. I cannot say how much it is.

According to the Auditor General's Report, the expenditure was $21,000 last year, and, as the salaries are rather small, most of that was spent in installation. If you have not any more installation to do, I cannot understand why you want $17,000 this year. The salaries would only amount to $6,000 or $7,000.
The salaries amounted to $7,850 ; rent, $1,200 ; banking commission, $1,000 ; and incidental expenses, including gas and stationery and many other things, $6,850.
Is this office to be a permanent charge on us of $17,000 a year, against whicn we are to get no revenue ?

It is more or less experimental for the present. We proceeded with it largely in contemplation of the fact that we would establish a mint, and the handling of the gold is a somewhat complicated process, so that it was necessary to establish an assay office in order that we might have some experience before we actually engaged in minting. The change in the method of collecting the royalty has decreased the business to a consider-Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
able extent, and the government have to consider the course it would adopt if the mint was not proceeded with immediately, and at the present time I am not in a position to say just exactly what course will be pursued.
Are the assay offices in other countries run free of charge ?

The assay office at Seattle is managed practically on the same principle.
Engraving, lithographing and printing maps of the Dominion and the North-west Territories, $15,000.
Is this something new ?

This is for maps which it is desired to issue during the coming year, consisting of :	engraving, paper printing, &c..
5,000 copies of Ontario map (3 sheets) $2,000:	printing, paper, &c., maps of
Manitoba, Assiniboia, Saskatchewan and Alberta, 5,000 copies of each, $1,500; engraving, paper, printing, &c., 10.000 copies of three sheet map of Manitoba and North west Territories, $45,000; engraving, printing, &c., 5,000 copies of British Columbia railway belt map, $2,500; and $5,000 for the purpose of beginning on the preparation of what is called an economic atlas of Canada. It is a work which I think will commend itself to the judgment of the House. It is to be prepared under the supervision of the geographer of the department, who has been engaged during the last two or three years in connection with the large map of Canada which has been lately issued; and which I think the members of the House will agree is a work urgently needed and supplies a very serious and long felt want. It is now proposed to have compiled an economic atlas of Canada, that is to say, an atlas which shall as far as possible exhibit the natural resources of the country. The work will be very extensive, and will incorporate the following, utilizing the plates of the large and small maps of Canada as far as possible, thus reducing the cost to a minimum; an economic edition of the large map in blue and black, only adding to this in large lettering, mineral signs for mineral occurrences, notes regarding, agricultural and timber resources; a geological map; a relief map, showing the elevation of surfaces: a map showing canals, with details of each; maps showing telephone and telegraph lines, lighthouses; agricultural diagrams, showing the productions in different parts of the country; diagrams of exports; navigation diagrams; maps relating to population; and generally such economic information as can properly be put into a book of that kind. For the purpose of preliminary expenses in connection with the enterprise, we are asking for $5,000 this year.
Who is in charge of that work.

Mr. James White, the geographer of the department. He was for many years connected with the geological survey, and on the death of the former geographer, he was transferred to the Department of the Interior. The large map of Canada was prepared under his supervision. He is a very competent and able officer. This $5,000 is to be devoted to getting together the material for the atlas.
The bon. gentleman mentioned a large map of which he wanted a large quantity. What is the object of them ?
For general distribution.
There has been a very large distribution already, has there not ?

Of the large map I think we distributed 5,000. A considerable improvement was made in the second edition. Of that there has been as yet only a very small distribution, but 5,000 were ordered. I may say that my view, which I trust the members of the committee will endorse, is that a map of that kind should be as generally distributed as possible. The cost of printing a map, after the information is all compiled and the work done, is comparatively small, and it seems to me the department could do no better work than to disseminate accurate information regarding the country in that form. My bon. friend would be surprised to know the inquiries that we get for these maps, from school inspectors down to the smallest school children. I think the distribution of a first-class map of Canada, giving detailed information, and showing the geographical features of the country, is among the most valuable work the department can do. I have given instructions therefore to be as liberal as possible in the distribution of the map.

I believe in that. There are a great many of the expenditures of my hon. friend's department that I would find fault with more readily than with this one. Who has charge of the work of printing these maps ?

The printing of this map was done by the Toronto Lithographing Company. That is
the only firm in Canada which has a staff of copper engravers. There has never before been a detailed map of the whole of Canada issued. The maps of the whole of Canada have hitherto been sketch maps. But this is a detailed map on which the attempt is made to give all the geographical information which would be given in a map of each province. In order to accomplish that, it is necessary to do fine work, which must be done by engraving on copper. Some years ago the Toronto Lithographing Company brought to Canada a small staff of
copper engravers, and they are practically occupied with the work given to them by the government. They are doing the work under the direction of Mr. White, the geographer.
Government of the Yukon Territory, $405,000.
What is the large appropriation stated in the estimates as not required this year ?

That is somewhat misleading as it will probably appear in the supplementary estimates. The information on which to base the item was not in the hands of the department when the estimates were being considered.
With regard to item 192, I would ask the hon. minister if he would not reserve these votes, one of which relates to schools, in order to allow of our discussing
It will not be necessary, because there is an item in the supplementary estimates dn which we can discuss the whole question.
I think it would be better to keep this item. We have passed some very large votes for my hon. friend, and we might keep this item for a later date.

There is no necessity for my hon. friend to reserve it, because there is an item in the supplementary estimates on which he can discuss anything that can be discussed on this. So, we shall be in the same position.
I refer to the vote for the North-west Territories.

Very well.
